religion: Buddhism (Mahayana) with Confucian governance and Daoist court ritual

population_estimates.note: Post-rebellion census wildly undercounts the unruly south.

description: The Tang Dynasty (618–907) is widely regarded as the cultural and imperial high point of medieval China. From its capital at Chang'an, the largest city in the world at the time, with over a million inhabitants, the dynasty governed via the most sophisticated bureaucracy of the early medieval period, recruited through the imperial examination system. Tang armies projected power into Central Asia along the Silk Road, defeating the Western Turks and dominating the Tarim Basin until the An Lushan Rebellion (755–763) shattered central authority. The dynasty patronised Buddhist monasticism, saw the maturation of classical Chinese poetry (Li Bai, Du Fu), and transmitted Chinese script, Confucian governance, and Buddhism into Korea, Japan, and Vietnam. After centuries of regional warlord rule following An Lushan, the dynasty collapsed in 907.

internal_structure.administrative_system: Three Departments and Six Ministries (sanshengliubu) with prefectural-county hierarchy

lifecycle_phases.description: Li Yuan establishes the dynasty from Sui-era civil war; Taizong consolidates.
Reigns of Taizong and Xuanzong; westward expansion into Tarim Basin and Sogdia; Buddhist golden age.
An Lushan Rebellion shatters central rule; jiedushi warlords rise; eunuch factionalism at court.
Huang Chao rebellion sacks Chang'an; Zhu Wen deposes the last Tang emperor.

rise_factors.description: Imperial examination system recruited talent meritocratically and produced a stable administrative class.
Fubing militia system combined agricultural settlement with frontier defense, sustaining campaigns into Central Asia.
Capital at Chang'an served as the eastern terminus of the Silk Road, generating massive customs revenue.
Patronage of Buddhism, Daoism, and Confucianism in parallel created a cosmopolitan intellectual climate.

decline_factors.description: Post-755 jiedushi military governors became hereditary regional warlords beyond central control.
An Lushan Rebellion (755–763) devastated the heartland; census figures dropped by tens of millions.
Loss of grain-tribute revenue from rebellious provinces starved the central treasury.
Late Tang droughts and famines triggered the Huang Chao rebellion (874–884), gutting the south.

key_figures.name: Wu Zetian
key_figures.notes: Only woman to formally rule China as emperor in her own name.

key_figures.name: Xuanzong (Li Longji)
key_figures.notes: Reign saw both cultural apogee and the An Lushan disaster.

key_figures.name: An Lushan
key_figures.notes: Military governor whose revolt broke the dynasty.

religion_composition.label: Confucianism (state ideology)
religion_composition.note: Confucianism functioned as official state philosophy, not exclusive of Buddhism/Daoism.

economic.primary_base: agriculture (wet-rice in south, millet/wheat in north)
